5.5 RECOGNITION OF PRIOR LEARNING WITHIN TVET
Recognition of Prior Learning is a process that recognizes a learner’s current
competencies which may have been achieved through means that include any
combination of formal or informal training and education, work experience or general
life experience. Recognition of uncertified learning may be combined with any formal
certification to enable assessment decisions to be made. The national vocational
qualifications system shall recognise prior learning based on national competency
standards and determine the extent to which an individual has achieved the required
competencies for partial or total completion of a national vocational qualification.The
NVQSL Provides RPL only up to NVQ level 4.

Recognition of prior learning shall be accessible to anyone with relevant competencies
achieved through means mentioned earlier that can be validated against the national
competency standards. in the absence of any formal training, the minimum industrial
exposure requirement to become eligible for RPL is stated in the relevant NVQ

This is likely to be the main expectation of the people you interview. You must therefore acquire real expertise and fluency in these subjects. The use of job search tools is almost obligatory for any adult seeking paid employment. This often takes the form of a CV to apply in response to published vacancies, or the submission of unsolicited applications. X Understanding and exploiting the labour market
Depending on the country, only 10 to 40 per cent of recruitments are published as job advertisements.
This may be through the Public Employment Service, private employment or temp agencies, the
press, specialized websites or social networks. This is the so-called “open market”
the recruitment opportunities are visible to all. On the other hand, the “hidden market” includes all
recruitments that are made without the employer publishing a job offer. Positions are filled either
through networking or through unsolicited applications.
It is important to understand that if an employer does not advertise their need for recruitment by
advertising a job offer, it is usually because they do not need to. Indeed, as soon as a position is available
in a company or organization (creation or resignation), this information will quickly become known
to its staff, its suppliers and its customers. It will be relayed through various networks: employees,
family, friends and so on. It is likely that profiles will thus be offered directly to the recruiter by their
own employees or their own network. Moreover, the company director regularly receives unsolicited
applications, and it is often sufficient to contact these people to find the right candidate. It is therefore
only if no direct application satisfies them that the recruiter will feel the need to advertise a job. This is
often the case for highly qualified positions for which profiles are scarce on the labour market.
Jobseekers generally limit themselves to exploiting the open market (and often not exhaustively). By
doing so, they depriving themselves of many employment opportunities. As an employment counsellor,
you should help them understand how the labour market works and encourage them to make the most
of all its facets: unsolicited applications, information monitoring, networking and so on.
